content: TEAD1, also known as Transcriptional Enhancer Factor TEF-1, TEA Domain Family Member 1, or Transcription Factor 13 (TCF-13), is a protein encoded by the TEAD1 gene in humans. It was the first identified member of the TEAD family of transcription factors. Structure All TEAD family members share a highly conserved DNA-binding domain known as the TEA domain. This domain recognizes a specific DNA sequence, 5’-CATTCCA/T-3’, referred to as the MCAT element. The three-dimensional structure of the TEA domain has been elucidated, revealing a conformation similar to that of the homeodomain, consisting of three α-helices (H1, H2, and H3). The H3 helix is responsible for the DNA-binding capability of TEAD proteins. Additionally, TEAD1 contains a conserved domain at its C-terminus, which facilitates the binding of cofactors. This domain is often referred to as the YAP1-binding domain, as it was identified through its interaction with YAP1, a well-known cofactor of TEAD proteins. Importantly, TEAD proteins cannot independently induce gene expression; they require association with cofactors to exert their transcriptional activity. Tissue Distribution TEAD1 is expressed in a variety of tissues, including skeletal muscle, pancreas, placenta, lung, and heart. Orthologs TEAD proteins are evolutionarily conserved and perform diverse functions across different organisms. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast), TEC-1 regulates the transposable element TY1 and is involved in pseudohyphal growth under nutrient-poor conditions. In Aspergillus nidulans, the TEA domain protein ABAA regulates the differentiation of conidiophores. In Drosophila melanogaster (fruit flies), the transcription factor Scalloped is essential for wing disc development, cell survival, and growth. In Xenopus (frogs), the TEAD1 ortholog has been shown to regulate muscle differentiation. Functions TEAD1 plays critical roles in various biological processes, including: Heart development, particularly in myocardium differentiation. Skeletal muscle development, including the regulation of skeletal muscle alpha-actin. Smooth muscle development, including the regulation of smooth muscle alpha-actin. Regulation of myosin heavy chain genes and cardiac muscle-specific genes such as troponin T and I. Control of cell proliferation. Regulation of apoptosis. Post-Transcriptional Modifications TEAD1 undergoes several post-transcriptional modifications that influence its function: Phosphorylation by Protein Kinase A (PKA): PKA phosphorylates TEAD1 at serine 102, located after the TEA domain. This modification is essential for the transcriptional activation of the α-myosin heavy chain (α-MyHC) gene. Phosphorylation by Protein Kinase C (PKC): PKC phosphorylates TEAD1 on serine and threonine residues near the last alpha loop of the TEA domain. This reduces TEAD1’s ability to bind the GTIIC enhancer. Palmitoylation: TEAD1 can be palmitoylated on a conserved cysteine residue at its C-terminus. This modification is crucial for the proper folding and stability of TEAD proteins. Cofactors TEAD proteins require cofactors to activate the transcription of target genes. TEAD1 interacts with various cofactors, including: SRC Family: TEAD1 interacts with all members of the steroid receptor coactivator (SRC) family. In HeLa cells, TEAD1 and SRC together induce gene expression. PARP (Poly-ADP Ribose Polymerase): TEAD1 interacts with PARP to regulate smooth muscle alpha-actin expression. PARP can also ADP-ribosylate TEAD proteins, modifying the chromatin environment to favor transcription through histone modification. SRF (Serum Response Factor): TEAD1 and SRF collaborate to regulate gene expression. MEF2 (Myocyte Enhancer Factor 2): TEAD1 physically interacts with MEF2. MEF2 binding to DNA enhances TEAD1 recruitment to MCAT sequences adjacent to MEF2 binding sites, leading to repression of the MLC2v (Myosin Light Chain 2v) and βMHC (β-myosin heavy chain) promoters. MAX: TEAD1 forms a complex with the phosphoprotein MAX, which regulates α-myosin heavy chain (α-MHC) gene expression. VGLL Proteins: All four Vestigial-like (VGLL) proteins interact with TEAD proteins. For instance, TEAD/VGLL1 complexes promote anchorage-independent cell proliferation in prostate cancer cell lines, suggesting a role in cancer progression. VGLL2 interaction with TEAD1 activates muscle promoters during C2C12 differentiation and enhances MyoD-mediated myogenesis in 10T1/2 cells. The TEAD/VGLL4 complex acts as a default transcriptional repressor. YAP and TAZ: TEAD proteins interact with YAP (Yes-Associated Protein 65) and TAZ (a paralog of YAP) both in vitro and in vivo. These interactions enhance TEAD transcriptional activity. YAP and TAZ are effectors of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway, which restricts organ growth by regulating cell proliferation and promoting apoptosis in mammals and Drosophila. Role in Cancer TEAD1 is dysregulated in various cancers, as revealed by transcriptome analyses. For example: In Kaposi sarcoma, TEAD1 levels are increased by 300-fold. Elevated TEAD expression is observed in basal-like breast cancers, fallopian tube carcinoma, and germ cell tumors. Conversely, TEAD expression is decreased in other breast cancer subtypes, as well as in renal and bladder cancers. This dual role may be attributed to the differential regulation of target genes by TEAD transcription factors. Additionally, recent studies have shown that TEAD1 and YAP promote cell stemness and chemoresistance in ovarian cancer. Genetic variants of TEAD proteins and YAP are enriched in certain cancers, further implicating their role in tumorigenesis.
